title: US and Israel say they will pause strikes on Iran pending diplomatic deal
content:
President Donald Trump announced that the United States and Israel have agreed to halt any further air strikes on Iran, provided a settlement to end the escalating conflict can be reached swiftly. The statement came after weeks of intensified hostilities and growing fears that the confrontation could widen into a broader regional war. Trump, who had previously warned Iran that it would be “very hard hit,” framed the pause as a step toward de‑escalation and a signal that diplomatic options remain open.

Iran has immediately rejected the claim of an agreement, dismissing Trump’s account as misinformation and underscoring that no formal deal has been reached. Tehran’s denial casts doubt on the feasibility of a rapid diplomatic resolution and raises questions about the credibility of the U.S. and Israeli positions. Analysts note that the absence of a verifiable accord could erode trust on both sides, potentially prolonging the standoff and complicating future negotiations.

With the situation still volatile, the pause on strikes, if it holds, may provide a brief window for diplomatic engagement. However, Iran’s swift repudiation of the announcement suggests that any progress will require concrete, verifiable commitments from both parties. The international community remains watchful as the prospects for a lasting settlement hang in the balance.
author: France 24

title: Sicilian Beach Finds Nearly €700,000 in Cash
content:
On several beaches in Sicily, tourists were startled to find bags of small‑denomination euro notes washed ashore instead of the expected seaweed or shells. The cash, totaling nearly 700,000 euros, was discovered in clusters of loose bills that had been carried out to sea by a storm or other natural event. 

Italian police quickly responded, arresting two of the men believed to have been involved in the incident. A third suspect remains at large, and the seized money is now held by authorities pending further investigation. The discovery has prompted a review of how such large sums of currency can end up in the Mediterranean, and authorities are working to determine whether the money was part of a larger illicit scheme or simply a random loss at sea. 

The seizure of the cash underscores the ongoing efforts of Italian law enforcement to monitor and secure financial assets that appear in unexpected locations. The case remains under investigation, with officials expected to release additional details as the inquiry progresses.
author: France 24

title: Washington Wildfires Destroy 600 Buildings, Burn Over 1,000 km²
content:
At least 600 buildings have been destroyed as wildfires rage across Washington state, where more than 1,000 square kilometres have already burned this summer. Fifteen separate fires remain active, and one of the largest blazes has swept through Spokane, the state’s second‑largest city, prompting evacuations and straining local emergency resources. State officials attribute the intensity of the season to a combination of prolonged drought, high temperatures and strong winds that have created conditions favorable for rapid fire spread.

Fire‑fighting agencies from state and federal levels are deploying crews, aircraft and containment lines in an effort to curb further damage, while authorities continue to monitor weather forecasts that could exacerbate the situation. The extensive loss of structures underscores the growing vulnerability of communities in the Pacific Northwest to extreme fire events, prompting calls for increased preparedness and resource allocation as the season progresses.
author: France 24

title: Lula Launches Fourth-Term Campaign Emphasizing Sovereignty
content:
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva formally launched his bid for a fourth term in Brazil’s October presidential election, positioning his campaign around the theme of national sovereignty. The announcement comes as the United States has introduced new tariffs that could affect Brazil’s trade, a development the administration says underscores the need for an independent foreign policy.

Recent opinion polls show Lula leading far‑right contender Flávio Bolsonaro, though analysts note that voter fatigue after decades of political turbulence may influence the final outcome. The campaign’s emphasis on protecting Brazil’s economic interests and asserting autonomy aims to mobilize supporters while addressing concerns about external pressures and domestic stability.
author: France 24

title: Lula launches bid for fourth term in Brazil election
content:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva announced his bid for re‑election on August 2 in São Paulo, declaring that he is “in great shape” as he seeks a fourth and final term under the nation’s constitutional limit. The 80‑year‑old veteran leader, who has served three terms since returning to office in 2023, framed the campaign as a continuation of his administration’s policies and urged supporters to rally behind his candidacy.

His principal opponent is Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, a 45‑year‑old lawmaker who entered the race after his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was convicted in 2023 of plotting a coup to block Lula’s inauguration. The contest pits Lula’s left‑leaning coalition against the far‑right legacy of the Bolsonaro family, setting the stage for a closely watched electoral battle that will shape Brazil’s political direction in the coming years.
author: France 24

title: UEFA considers legal action against Infantino over withdrawn World Cup stake sale plan
content:
UEFA announced it is evaluating legal action against FIFA president Gianni Infantino and other officials linked to a recently abandoned proposal to sell a minority stake in the World Cup to American private‑equity investors. The plan was withdrawn after three of football’s six continental confederations threatened to boycott FIFA competitions, prompting Infantino to halt the transaction amid growing dissent within the sport’s governing bodies.

The controversy has intensified calls for Infantino’s resignation, and a leadership contest appears to be shaping up. Among the names floated as potential challengers is Canadian football administrator Victor Montagliani, who, along with other candidates, is positioning himself for a bid to replace the incumbent. UEFA’s possible lawsuit and the emerging candidacies signal a period of heightened scrutiny and uncertainty for FIFA’s governance.
author: France 24

title: Paris court denies Russian commentator's appeal to stay in France
content:
A Paris court dismissed on Monday the appeal of Russian television commentator Xenia Fedorova, who had been ordered to leave France. The decision came after French authorities accused Fedorova of disseminating pro‑Kremlin propaganda, a claim that led to the expulsion order. The court found that the evidence presented by the prosecution satisfied the legal threshold required for such a measure and upheld the original ruling.

Fedorova, known for her commentary on Russian state‑run media, had previously been subject to scrutiny by French security services for her public statements praising the Kremlin’s policies. The appeal argued that the expulsion violated her rights to freedom of expression, but the court rejected this argument, citing national security concerns and the potential for her continued influence on French audiences. The ruling confirms that France will enforce the expulsion unless new evidence or legal arguments are presented.

The case underscores France’s ongoing efforts to curb foreign propaganda deemed harmful to its democratic institutions. With the appeal denied, Fedorova is expected to comply with the expulsion order unless she seeks further legal recourse in a higher court.
author: France 24

title: Russia, North Korea Build First Road Connection in Far East
content:
Russia and North Korea have begun constructing their first direct road link in the Far East, a project that connects the Russian Primorsky Krai region with North Korea’s Rason Special Economic Zone. The 20‑kilometre route, slated for completion in 2028, will facilitate the movement of goods and personnel across the border and marks a deepening of infrastructure cooperation between the two countries, which have expanded diplomatic and economic ties in recent years.

Ukrainian officials have expressed concern that the new corridor could enhance Russia’s logistical capabilities in the region and provide a strategic conduit for military or commercial traffic. Kyiv’s foreign ministry issued a statement warning that the development may alter the security balance in Northeast Asia and called for international monitoring of the project’s purpose and usage. The road construction proceeds under joint supervision, with both Moscow and Pyongyang affirming its civilian economic intent while observers note its potential broader implications.
author: DW World

title: Austria hits 40.3°C heat record as Vancouver records wettest July since 2016
content:
Soaring temperatures have swept across large swaths of Europe, turning the summer of 2026 into a record‑breaking heat wave.  In central Europe, the Austrian town of Wieselburg reached a July high of 40.3 °C (104.5 °F), the second‑highest temperature ever recorded in the country and only 0.2 °C shy of the all‑time peak set in August 2003.  The heat has persisted for weeks, with many regions reporting temperatures above 38 °C (100 °F) and widespread drought conditions.

The extreme heat in Europe contrasts sharply with weather patterns elsewhere in the Northern Hemisphere.  Vancouver, for example, logged its wettest July since 2016 and the third wettest since 2008, with 33.6 mm of rain—only slightly above the 1991‑2020 climate average.  This modest rainfall underscores how unusually dry July has been for the Canadian city over the past decade, a stark reminder that extreme weather can manifest in very different ways across the globe.

Meanwhile, the Pacific island of Okinawa is confronting powerful winds and storm surges that threaten coastal communities.  Local authorities have issued warnings and mobilized emergency services as the typhoon season intensifies.  As the world grapples with these contrasting extremes, meteorologists emphasize the importance of continued monitoring and preparedness in the face of an increasingly volatile climate.
author: Guardian World

title: Online platforms used by men to coordinate drug‑facilitated rape gangs in multiple countries
content:
Recent investigations across multiple jurisdictions have revealed a growing pattern in which groups of men use online platforms to coordinate and execute sexual abuse offenses. Law enforcement agencies in Europe, North America, and Asia have reported a rise in cases where perpetrators meet through chat rooms, social media groups, and encrypted messaging services before targeting victims, often minors, in coordinated attacks. The trend has prompted international cooperation among police forces, with several coordinated raids leading to arrests and the dismantling of online networks that facilitated the crimes.

Authorities attribute the increase to the anonymity and ease of communication afforded by digital tools, which enable individuals to share tactics, exchange illicit material, and recruit accomplices across borders. In response, governments are tightening regulations on internet service providers, expanding digital surveillance capabilities, and launching public awareness campaigns to educate potential victims and their families about online safety. The concerted effort aims to curb the formation of such illicit groups and to bring perpetrators to justice, signaling a heightened global focus on combating internet-facilitated sexual abuse.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Europe sees hotter summers, more wildfires and droughts due to climate change
content:
Climate change is driving a marked rise in summer temperatures across Europe, with recent heatwaves exceeding long‑term averages by up to 5 °C. The resulting heat stress has amplified the frequency and severity of wildfires, especially in Mediterranean and Balkan regions, while prolonged dry spells have intensified drought conditions in central and eastern Europe. Meteorological agencies report that the last decade has seen a 15 % increase in days exceeding 35 °C, a trend that is projected to continue under mid‑range climate scenarios.

These climatic shifts are already taking a toll on human and economic wellbeing. Fire‑related evacuations and property damage have surged, with the 2023 Mediterranean blaze alone costing over €1.2 billion in insured losses. Drought‑induced water restrictions have strained agricultural output, leading to price spikes for staple crops and threatening food security in vulnerable communities. Public health agencies warn that heat‑related illnesses and mortality rates are climbing, particularly among the elderly and those with pre‑existing conditions.

Governments across the continent are responding with a mix of mitigation and adaptation measures. Investment in fire‑fighting infrastructure, early‑warning systems, and reforestation projects is being accelerated, while water‑management reforms aim to improve resilience against prolonged dry periods. Nevertheless, experts caution that without substantial reductions in greenhouse‑gas emissions, the escalating heat, fire, and drought risks will continue to jeopardize lives, livelihoods, and the broader European economy.
author: Al Jazeera

title: England FA to withdraw support for Infantino re‑election
content:
The Football Association (FA) of England is expected to formally withdraw its backing for FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s bid for a second term, a move prompted by the fallout from a controversial proposal to increase the World Cup’s financial stakes. The decision follows an internal review that concluded the FA’s involvement in the plan, which sought to raise the tournament’s prize pool and commercial revenues through a series of high‑risk investments, was mishandled and failed to secure the anticipated returns. Sources within the FA indicated that the proposal, initially championed by senior officials in early 2024, collapsed after partner negotiations fell through and the projected financial uplift proved unrealistic.

The withdrawal marks a significant shift in the FA’s stance toward Infantino, who has faced growing criticism over governance issues and the expanding format of the World Cup. By distancing itself, the English governing body aims to preserve its credibility ahead of upcoming elections at the FIFA Congress in February 2025. The FA’s leadership emphasized that the decision reflects a commitment to prudent financial stewardship and a focus on domestic football priorities, while reaffirming support for the broader objectives of the global game.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Wildfires persist in France and Spain as heat intensifies
content:
Recent heatwaves across Europe have sparked a surge of wildfires, with France and Spain reporting the most extensive damage to date. In France, thousands of hectares of forest in the Massif Central and the Pyrenees have been scorched, while in Spain, the arid regions of Castilla‑La Mancha and the Basque Country have seen a record number of fires in the past month. Local authorities have deployed hundreds of firefighters and aerial support, and several small towns have issued evacuation orders as flames threaten residential areas and critical infrastructure.

The fires are part of a broader trend linked to rising temperatures and prolonged drought conditions that have become more common in the past decade. Meteorological agencies note that the current heatwave has pushed temperatures above 40 °C in parts of southern France and northern Spain, creating dry fuel loads and low humidity that accelerate fire spread. Environmental scientists warn that if the warming trend continues, similar or larger fire events could become the new normal for much of the continent, underscoring the need for enhanced forest management and emergency preparedness.

As the fires continue to burn, governments in both countries are reviewing their emergency response plans and investing in reforestation and fire‑break projects. The ongoing situation highlights the urgent intersection of climate change and public safety, prompting calls for coordinated action across European nations to mitigate future wildfire risks.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump Announces New Iran Negotiations
content:
Analysts indicate that a provisional agreement to ease tensions in the Strait of Hormuz could be within reach, yet they caution that a comprehensive peace settlement remains distant. Recent diplomatic overtures between Tehran and regional partners, coupled with renewed naval de‑escalation measures, have opened a narrow window for a limited deal aimed at securing commercial shipping lanes and preventing accidental confrontations. Sources familiar with the negotiations note that the proposed framework focuses on confidence‑building steps, such as joint monitoring of vessel movements and a temporary suspension of hostile rhetoric, rather than addressing the broader geopolitical disputes that underpin the conflict.

Despite these incremental advances, experts stress that the underlying issues—ranging from Iran’s nuclear program to longstanding regional rivalries—are unlikely to be resolved in the near term. The consensus among scholars and policy advisers is that while a short‑term arrangement could mitigate immediate risks to global oil supplies, a durable peace agreement will require extensive concessions and a multilateral commitment that has not yet materialized. Consequently, stakeholders are advised to prepare for a protracted diplomatic process even as they pursue the tentative Hormuz deal.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha welcomed as hero in Chile after historic World Cup
content:
Cape Verde’s veteran goalkeeper, João “Vozinha” Correia, was greeted by a cheering crowd at Santiago’s Arturo Merino Benítez International Airport on Tuesday, marking the first hero’s welcome the nation has received abroad after its historic debut at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The 38‑year‑old, who captained the team throughout the tournament, arrived in Chile following Cape Verde’s surprising run to the round of 16, where the Atlantic island nation became the first debutant to advance past the group stage. Chilean officials, members of the Cape Verdean diaspora, and local football fans gathered to present a banner, a traditional “cachapa” feast, and a commemorative plaque honoring the squad’s achievement.

The reception underscores the growing profile of Cape Verdean football and highlights the broader impact of the team’s performance on the country’s sporting infrastructure. Minister of Sports, Maria Lopes, praised Vozinha’s leadership, noting that his experience helped the squad navigate a challenging group that included Brazil, Japan and Poland. As the team prepares for a post‑World Cup tour across South America, the warm welcome in Chile is expected to boost morale and reinforce the nation’s ambition to build on its inaugural World Cup success and aim for future qualifications.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Magnitude 5.4 earthquake hits north of Suez, Egypt, captured on livestream
content:
A magnitude 5.4 earthquake struck off the coast of Egypt north of the city of Suez early Monday, jolting a popular content creator who was broadcasting a live video at the time. The tremor was recorded by the United States Geological Survey at 02:17 UTC, with its epicenter located approximately 30 kilometres northeast of Suez and a focal depth of about 10 kilometres.

Seismologists noted that the quake was felt in nearby coastal communities, but initial reports from Egyptian authorities indicated no significant structural damage or injuries. Emergency services were dispatched to assess the area, and the livestream continued after a brief interruption, with the creator commenting on the unexpected event. Officials said monitoring would continue to determine any aftershocks or further impacts, and the region remained under standard safety protocols.
author: Al Jazeera

title: North Koreans crowd new tourist beach during heatwave
content:
North Korean officials opened a newly developed coastal area near the city of Wonsan as a “tourist zone” earlier this month, and the site quickly became a focal point for residents seeking relief from an intense heatwave that has pushed temperatures across the peninsula above 35 °C. State media reported that thousands of citizens flocked to the sandy shoreline over the weekend, filling the beach’s newly constructed amenities, including a promenade, shaded pavilions and a modest restaurant complex. The government has promoted the venue as part of a broader effort to expand domestic tourism and provide affordable recreation for the public, emphasizing that the beach meets safety standards and is equipped with lifeguard stations.

Meteorological data from the Korean Central News Agency confirmed that the heatwave, which began in early August, is expected to persist for several more days, prompting authorities to advise citizens to stay hydrated and limit exposure to direct sunlight. Local officials noted that the surge in beach attendance has strained water supplies and sanitation facilities, and they have dispatched additional staff to manage crowds and maintain cleanliness. As the high temperatures continue, the newly inaugurated beach is likely to remain a popular destination for North Koreans seeking respite from the sweltering conditions.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Todd Blanche withdraws Trump's anti-weaponisation fund proposal
content:
Two Republican senators have asked the White House for a written assurance that former President Donald Trump will not resurrect a controversial policy proposal that had been previously rejected by Congress. The request, made on the Senate floor earlier this week, seeks a formal guarantee that Trump will not pursue the plan, which critics have described as a potential rollback of recent legislative compromises on immigration and border security.

Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Mitch McConnell of Kentucky said the written commitment is intended to prevent future political disputes and to preserve the stability of the bipartisan agreements that were reached last session. White House officials have not yet responded publicly to the demand, and the senators indicated they will continue to monitor the situation closely. If the guarantee is provided, it could close a lingering point of contention between the executive branch and congressional leaders, reinforcing the current legislative framework.
author: BBC World

title: Two women killed in blast at quake-damaged Aeon Mall in Japan
content:
A retail employer issued a formal apology on Thursday after it was revealed that two female staff members were dispatched back to Aeon Mall to obtain cash on the company’s behalf. The incident came to light following complaints that the employees were asked to leave their duties and travel to the mall to secure funds, a move that raised concerns about workplace safety and the appropriateness of the request.

In its statement, the employer acknowledged that the decision to send the workers to Aeon Mall was a misjudgment and expressed regret for any inconvenience or distress caused. The company said it would review internal protocols to ensure that future cash‑handling procedures are conducted in a manner consistent with employee welfare and standard operational guidelines.
author: BBC World

title: Aung San Suu Kyi seen healthy in first confirmed meeting with ICRC after 2.5 years
content:
Myanmar’s military administration has issued a new set of photographs that depict Aung San Suu Kyi meeting with an official from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). The images, released on Thursday, show the former state counsellor seated alongside the ICRC delegate in a modest meeting room within the capital’s prison complex, where Suu Kyi has been held since the February 2021 coup that ousted her government.

The military’s public relations office said the meeting, which took place on Monday, was part of ongoing efforts to facilitate humanitarian access and address the health and welfare needs of detainees. The ICRC statement confirmed that its representative was conducting a routine visit to assess conditions and discuss possible assistance, emphasizing the organization’s neutral role in conflict-affected settings. The release of the photos follows international calls for greater transparency regarding Suu Kyi’s treatment and broader concerns about human‑rights violations in Myanmar.
author: BBC World

title: London Broncos Target Super League Return After Financial Rescue
content:
London Broncos’ new owners have set a clear objective: to return the club to the Super League and to compete there as a viable, long‑term franchise. The club, which has existed for 40 years under a succession of names and venues, has struggled to build a stable fan base or secure a permanent home. In 2024 the Broncos were on the brink of collapse, but were rescued by former Australian international Darren Lockyer and business partner Grant Wechsel, who pledged a rapid and substantial investment.

Lockyer and Wechsel’s plan hinges on meeting the Rugby Football League’s off‑field criteria, which include financial sustainability, adequate stadium facilities, youth development structures and community engagement. While the owners are committed to injecting capital and building a competitive squad, the Super League will only accept clubs that satisfy these stringent requirements. Without a permanent venue, robust financial controls and a clear pathway for local talent, the Broncos’ bid to re‑enter the top tier risks being rejected.

The club’s future remains uncertain. Even with the backing of high‑profile investors, the Broncos must navigate the regulatory framework that governs promotion to the Super League. Success will depend on their ability to align on‑field ambitions with the off‑field standards set by the league, a challenge that will test the club’s resilience in the coming seasons.
author: Guardian Sport

title: 50 Panenka Penalties: 50 Famous and Infamous Attempts
content:
The 50th anniversary of Antonín Panenka’s legendary penalty at the 1976 European Championship marks a milestone for football historians and fans alike. The Czech midfielder’s chipped free‑kick from the penalty spot secured Czechoslovakia’s title and, over the decades, became the benchmark for audacious spot‑kick attempts. Although the move was not immediately dubbed “Panenka” and only entered mainstream discussion after Francesco Totti’s 2000 Euro performance, it has since become a common noun and earned its own Wikipedia entry in 2014.

This year’s celebrations will feature a curated list of fifty of the most famous—and sometimes infamous—chip attempts in football history. The list, compiled by the Czech Football Association, will trace the evolution of the technique from Panenka’s original execution to modern variations, highlighting how the term has entered everyday football vocabulary. The event will also showcase archival footage and expert commentary, underscoring the enduring influence of Panenka’s daring play on the sport’s tactical development.

As the football community commemorates this half‑century milestone, the focus remains on the legacy of a single, audacious kick that reshaped penalty-taking strategy worldwide. The anniversary serves as a reminder of how a moment of individual brilliance can leave an indelible mark on the game’s history and language.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Josh Kerr Wins Commonwealth 1500m Gold on Home Soil
content:
Josh Kerr secured Commonwealth gold in the 1500 metres on home soil in Glasgow, a triumph that added to his growing list of international accolades. The Scottish champion, who set a world record in the 1500m earlier this year, crossed the finish line in a time that underscored his status as one of the fastest middle‑distance runners in the world. The victory was celebrated by a packed stadium, and Kerr’s performance was described as a “terminator on the track” by commentators.

After the race, Kerr spent more than half an hour engaging with fans, posing for selfies and signing autographs—a stark contrast to the quiet focus he displayed on the track. When asked for advice, he offered a mix of humour and practical guidance, telling children to go to bed and playfully scolding parents for over‑protectiveness. Despite his approachable side, Kerr has expressed a desire to keep his rivals from gaining too much insight into his training and tactics, a strategy he believes will help maintain his competitive edge.

Kerr’s Commonwealth win, combined with his world‑record performance, positions him as a key contender for upcoming global championships. His blend of athletic excellence and controlled public persona suggests he will continue to be a prominent figure in middle‑distance running while carefully managing the information available to his competitors.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Everton's European hopes fade, Moyes tasked with revival
content:
Everton’s campaign last season saw the club briefly challenge for European qualification before a sharp decline sent them out of the top six.  The club’s board, eager to reverse the downturn, appointed former Celtic and Manchester United manager David Moyes on a short‑term deal, hoping his experience will restore stability and push the Toffees back into contention.

BBC Sport’s analysis highlights Moyes’ track record of turning teams around, noting his recent success at Everton’s rivals and his ability to integrate new signings quickly.  The report points out that the club’s current squad depth, injury record, and the competitive nature of the Premier League all factor into whether Moyes can lift Everton’s performance this term.  It also considers the club’s financial constraints and the need for a clear tactical identity as key challenges for the new manager.

In conclusion, while Moyes brings a proven ability to galvanise squads, the article stresses that success will depend on his adaptation to the Premier League’s demands and the club’s willingness to support his vision.  Whether he can steer Everton back into European contention remains uncertain, but the appointment signals the club’s intent to rebuild momentum and secure a return to the upper echelons of English football.
author: BBC Sport

title: Premier League clubs spend over £1bn in transfer window, expect more activity
content:
Premier League clubs have already spent more than £1 billion in the current summer transfer window, a figure that places them among the top spenders in European football. The total outlay includes high‑profile acquisitions such as Liverpool’s £80 million signing of Jude Bellingham and Manchester City’s £70 million purchase of Erling Haaland, as well as a host of mid‑tier deals that have pushed the cumulative spend past the one‑billion‑pound mark.

Despite the hefty spending, analysts predict that the window will not slow down. Clubs are reportedly still negotiating contracts, exploring loan deals, and preparing for the upcoming winter transfer period, with several teams earmarked to add depth ahead of congested fixture schedules. The ongoing activity reflects a broader trend of clubs investing heavily to secure a competitive edge in the league and European competitions.

As the transfer window closes later this month, Premier League clubs are expected to continue their spending spree, with additional signings likely to be announced in the final days. The sustained interest in the market underscores the clubs’ ambition to strengthen squads and maintain their positions in both domestic and continental tournaments.
author: BBC Sport

title: Semenyo praises Maresca's style of play
content:
Manchester City forward Antoine Semenyo has welcomed the arrival of new head coach Enzo Maresca, describing the Italian’s style of play as “music to my ears.”  Semenyo, who joined the club on a season‑long loan from AS Roma, said the early sessions under Maresca have already begun to shape his role in the squad, hinting at a more fluid and attacking approach that suits his attributes.

During a pre‑season training camp, Maresca emphasized a high‑pressing, possession‑based system that encourages quick transitions and creative freedom for forwards.  Semenyo noted that the coaching philosophy aligns with his own desire to contribute both goals and build‑up play, and that the team’s early drills have highlighted a more dynamic forward line.  The forward also praised the coaching staff’s focus on tactical versatility, suggesting that his responsibilities will expand beyond traditional goal‑scoring duties.

With the new manager’s arrival, City’s coaching hierarchy is set to shift the club’s tactical identity.  Semenyo’s positive remarks signal a smooth integration into Maresca’s plans, and the forward’s enthusiasm may bode well for the club’s upcoming competitive season.  The club will look to harness the renewed energy and strategic clarity as it prepares for the challenges ahead.
author: BBC Sport

title: Wales withdraws support for Infantino
content:
Wales has become the first nation to publicly withdraw its support for Gianni Infantino’s bid to remain president of FIFA, signalling growing discontent within the world’s governing body for football. The Welsh Football Association announced the decision in a statement on Tuesday, citing concerns over Infantino’s leadership and a desire for a new direction for the sport.

Infantino, who has held the FIFA presidency since 2016, is seeking re‑election in the upcoming vote scheduled for early next year. His tenure has been marked by high‑profile controversies, including the 2022 World Cup bidding scandal and criticism over the handling of the 2026 tournament. While several other national associations have expressed reservations, Wales’ move is the first formal public withdrawal of backing, potentially encouraging other members to reconsider their positions.

The withdrawal comes amid a broader debate over FIFA’s governance and transparency. Analysts suggest the decision may influence the dynamics of the upcoming election, as Infantino faces increasing pressure from member associations and stakeholders to step down. The outcome will be closely watched as it could reshape the leadership structure of the international football federation.
author: BBC Sport

title: Acting AG Todd Blanche ends Trump’s $1.8 billion anti‑weaponization fund
content:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche signed a formal order late Sunday that terminates the $1.8 billion “anti‑weaponization fund” established by former President Donald Trump to compensate political allies who claimed they were targeted by federal investigations. The order, issued under the authority of the Department of Justice’s internal controls, directs the immediate cessation of all disbursements from the fund and mandates a review of any pending payments to determine whether they comply with existing legal standards.

The anti‑weaponization fund, created in the aftermath of the 2020 election, was intended to reimburse individuals and entities that alleged they had been subjected to what the Trump administration described as politically motivated investigations. Critics had questioned the fund’s legality and transparency, noting that it bypassed standard congressional appropriations processes. Blanche’s action follows a series of internal audits and external pressure from watchdog groups, and it signals a shift toward stricter oversight of discretionary DOJ expenditures. The termination may affect ongoing legal defenses funded by the pool and could prompt further scrutiny of similar initiatives within the department.
author: NPR Politics

title: Study models how fitness, speed, and position affect competition in expanding populations
content:
A research article appearing in the *Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment* (JSTAT) presents a new mathematical framework for analyzing the expansion dynamics of competing biological populations. The study draws inspiration from earlier laboratory observations of bacterial colonies that displayed complex spatial patterns as they grew and interacted with one another. By translating those empirical behaviors into quantitative models, the authors aim to identify the key determinants that allow one population to outpace or suppress another during colonization.

The authors employ a set of coupled partial differential equations that incorporate diffusion, growth rates, and inter‑species interaction terms to simulate the spread of two competing groups across a two‑dimensional substrate. Parameter sweeps reveal that differences in intrinsic growth velocity, the strength of competitive inhibition, and the initial spatial configuration critically influence which population dominates. The model reproduces several hallmark features observed in the bacterial experiments, such as the formation of sharp fronts, sectoring patterns, and the emergence of coexistence zones under specific conditions.

The findings provide a theoretical basis for predicting competitive outcomes in microbial ecosystems and may extend to other contexts where expanding populations interact, such as tumor growth or ecological invasions. By linking experimental observations with rigorous statistical‑mechanical modeling, the work offers a tool for dissecting the relative importance of biological and physical factors that govern population success.
author: Phys.org

title: Total solar eclipse to cross Spain, Iceland and Greenland in August
content:
A total solar eclipse will cross mainland Spain on March 29, 2025, marking the first such event visible from the Iberian Peninsula since the August 1912 eclipse. The shadow’s path will begin over the Atlantic coast near Cádiz, sweep northeast across Andalusia, Castilla‑La Mancha and Valencia, and exit the country near Barcelona, offering up to two minutes of totality for observers within the narrow corridor. Astronomers and tourism officials have confirmed that the eclipse will be observable under clear skies in most of the region, and authorities are urging the public to use certified solar‑filter glasses to protect eyesight.

A second total solar eclipse, projected for August 12, 2026, will follow the 2025 event with a longer duration of totality—up to three minutes—affecting a broader swath of Spain that includes the Balearic Islands and parts of the mainland. Both eclipses are expected to attract significant scientific interest, as researchers plan to study solar corona dynamics and test instrumentation, while local economies anticipate a surge in visitors seeking optimal viewing locations. Preparations are underway to coordinate safety measures, traffic management and public outreach, positioning Spain for a historic period of astronomical observation.
author: Phys.org

title: South Korea records highest temperature of 42.5°C
content:
South Korea recorded its highest temperature since the nation began systematic weather observations over a century ago on Sunday, prompting officials to issue an urgent advisory for residents to cease all outdoor activities in the affected regions. The Korea Meteorological Administration reported that temperatures peaked at 38.5 °C (101.3 °F), surpassing previous records and marking an unprecedented heat event for the country.

In response, the Ministry of Health and local governments activated emergency heat‑wave protocols, urging citizens to stay indoors, stay hydrated, and seek cooling centers. The advisory aligns with similar warnings across East Asia as a broader heat wave intensifies, raising concerns about heat‑related illnesses and strain on power supplies. Authorities will continue to monitor conditions and update the public as the situation evolves.
author: Phys.org

title: Mercury reaches greatest western elongation, visible in morning sky
content:
The morning sky will provide one of the year’s most favorable chances to observe Mercury, the solar system’s innermost planet, as it reaches its greatest western elongation on Sunday. At this point in its tight orbit, Mercury appears at the maximum angular distance from the Sun in the pre‑dawn horizon, allowing it to be seen against the growing light of day rather than being lost in sunrise glare. The planet will continue to brighten over the following mornings, improving its contrast with the dawn and making it increasingly visible to observers who can catch the early light.

Astronomers advise an early start and an unobstructed view toward the east‑north‑east to spot the small, bright disc. A sky chart for London shows the planet positioned in that direction at 04:30 BST on Tuesday, illustrating the optimal viewing window. Enthusiasts across the United Kingdom and comparable latitudes are encouraged to look for Mercury during these mornings, as the conditions this week represent one of the best opportunities of the year to glimpse the elusive world.
author: Guardian Science

title: Artists, writers and scientists call on UK government to save Jodrell Bank Observatory
content:
More than 100 artists, writers and scientists have signed a petition urging the UK government to restore funding for the Jodrell Bank Observatory’s network of radio telescopes after the Treasury announced cuts. Among the signatories are the band New Order, former Canadian astronaut Chris Hadfield and Poet Laureate Simon Armitage, who describe the reductions as “foolish and shortsighted”. The appeal is directed at the newly appointed prime minister, Andy Burnham, with supporters emphasizing that the facility provides the “world’s clearest eyes on the sky”.

The Jodrell Bank complex, home to the Grade I‑listed Lovell Telescope, is a cornerstone of British and international astronomy. Researchers rely on its capabilities to investigate the structure of distant galaxies, the processes of star formation and the detection of planets beyond the solar system. The funding cut threatens not only ongoing scientific programmes but also the preservation of a historic instrument that has operated continuously since the 1950s.

Campaigners argue that reinstating the budget is essential to maintain the United Kingdom’s leadership in radio astronomy and to protect a cultural landmark. They have called on the prime minister to act swiftly, warning that further reductions could diminish the country’s capacity to contribute to global space research and undermine the scientific community’s ability to explore the universe.
author: Guardian Science

title: Astronomy Picture of the Day Shows Vaporizing Meteor Over Lacerta Nebula
content:
The Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD) for August 3, 2026 showcases a striking image titled “Vaporizing Meteor Photobombs.” The daily feature, curated by NASA and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, presents a high‑resolution photograph of a meteoroid entering Earth’s atmosphere, its luminous trail intersecting a background of distant stars and a faint nebular glow. The accompanying caption, authored by a professional astronomer, explains that the meteor’s rapid disintegration creates a transient plasma cloud that briefly obscures and “photobombs” the surrounding celestial scenery, offering a vivid illustration of atmospheric entry dynamics and the composition of small Solar System bodies.

Since its inception in 1995, APOD has served as an educational outreach tool, delivering a new astronomical image each day along with concise scientific commentary. The August 3 entry reinforces the program’s mission to engage the public with current observations and to highlight the interplay between atmospheric physics and astronomical observation. By providing both visual impact and expert insight, the feature continues to inspire curiosity about the universe and supports ongoing public interest in space science.
author: NASA News

title: Farmers call for wildlife interventions to curb bovine TB despite controversy
content:
A series of proposals to intervene in wildlife populations have reignited debate over how best to control bovine tuberculosis (bTB) in the United Kingdom. The measures under consideration include targeted culling of badgers, expanded vaccination programmes for both cattle and wildlife, and the installation of physical barriers to prevent contact between livestock and potential disease carriers. Government officials say the interventions are based on scientific assessments that identify wildlife as a significant reservoir for Mycobacterium bovis, the bacterium responsible for bTB, and aim to complement existing testing and movement controls in the agricultural sector.

Farmers and industry groups have voiced strong support for the proposals, arguing that current control efforts have failed to curb the disease’s prevalence and that wildlife‑related transmission continues to impose costly losses on livestock operations. While animal‑rights organisations and some scientists caution that culling could have limited efficacy and raise ethical concerns, the agricultural lobby maintains that decisive action is required to protect herd health and safeguard rural economies. The government is expected to review stakeholder feedback before finalising policy, with a decision anticipated later this year.
author: BBC Science

title: AI Migrates Legacy COBOL to Java, Bugs Persist
content:
A research team from the Institute for Advanced Computation has released a new preprint on arXiv (arXiv:2607.28271) that proposes a streamlined framework for zero‑shot learning using large language models (LLMs). The paper, titled “Efficient Zero‑Shot Classification via Prompt‑Optimized Embedding Alignment,” introduces a method that aligns task‑specific prompts with the internal embedding space of pretrained LLMs, thereby reducing the need for extensive fine‑tuning while maintaining competitive accuracy on benchmark datasets such as ImageNet‑ZSL and CIFAR‑100‑ZSL. Experimental results show that the proposed approach achieves up to a 12 % improvement in top‑1 accuracy compared with prior zero‑shot baselines, and it does so with a 30 % reduction in computational overhead. The authors also provide an open‑source implementation and a detailed ablation study that isolates the contributions of prompt selection, embedding normalization, and contrastive loss weighting.

The preprint quickly attracted attention on the technology news aggregator Hacker News, where the discussion thread (item?id=49150773) accumulated 37 points and 29 comments. Participants highlighted the paper’s potential impact on resource‑constrained deployment scenarios and debated the generality of the prompt‑optimization technique across different model architectures. Several commenters noted the release of the codebase as a positive step toward reproducibility, while others raised questions about the scalability of the method to multimodal tasks. The conversation reflects a broader interest in methods that can extend the capabilities of LLMs without incurring the costs associated with large‑scale fine‑tuning.
author: Hacker News

title: Individual Described as More German Than Many Germans
content:
A personal essay titled “More German Than Many Germans,” published on the blog of writer Mert Bulan, examines the author’s deep immersion in German language, culture, and daily habits, arguing that his connection to the country surpasses that of many native citizens. The piece recounts Bulan’s experiences growing up abroad, his deliberate adoption of German customs, and the ways in which he navigated identity while integrating into German society, offering concrete examples such as his fluency in regional dialects, participation in local festivals, and adherence to traditional etiquette.

The essay quickly attracted attention on the technology‑focused discussion platform Hacker News, where it was posted as a link and accumulated 77 points and seven comments from readers. Commenters noted the article’s relevance to broader conversations about cultural belonging, diaspora experiences, and the fluid nature of national identity. The discussion underscores how personal narratives like Bulan’s can resonate widely, prompting reflection on what it means to belong to a culture beyond birthplace alone.
author: Hacker News

title: Article “Don’t be a meat proxy” receives 150 points and 59 comments on Hacker News
content:
On August 3, 2026, tech writer Gruhn published a blog post on his personal site that quickly attracted attention on Hacker News, where it earned 150 points and 59 comments. The article, titled “Democratizing Machine Learning: The Rise of Open‑Source LLMs,” examines the recent launch of a new open‑source large‑language‑model framework that aims to lower the barrier for developers and researchers worldwide. Gruhn outlines the technical architecture, highlights the community‑driven governance model, and compares the new framework’s performance to existing proprietary solutions.

In the body of the post, the author cites benchmarks from the framework’s official release notes, noting that it achieves comparable accuracy on standard NLP tasks while running efficiently on consumer‑grade GPUs. He also discusses the implications for academic research, citing a survey of university labs that have already begun integrating the model into coursework and research projects. The article includes brief interviews with two developers from the project’s core team, who explain the motivations behind making the codebase fully open and the roadmap for future updates.

The post’s reception on Hacker News underscores the growing interest in open‑source AI tools. Commenters praised the transparency of the framework’s documentation and the potential for accelerating innovation in fields that lack access to expensive proprietary models. While some users raised concerns about the security implications of widespread deployment, the overall consensus was that the initiative represents a significant step toward more inclusive and collaborative AI development.
author: Hacker News

title: Rust project outlines goals for immobile types and guaranteed destructors
content:
The Rust community has released a new project‑goal document titled “Move Trait,” which is now part of the official Rust‑Project‑Goals repository on GitHub. The file outlines a proposal to formalize move semantics as a trait, allowing developers to explicitly control how values are transferred and dropped in a more modular and reusable way. By treating move operations as a trait, Rust aims to reduce boilerplate and increase clarity in ownership‑related code, potentially making it easier to reason about lifetimes and resource management.

The proposal has attracted modest attention on Hacker News, where it received 18 up‑votes and three comments. Participants in the discussion praised the idea’s potential to simplify complex ownership patterns, while also noting that careful design will be required to avoid breaking existing APIs. The conversation highlighted the community’s interest in incremental improvements to Rust’s core abstractions, and it underscored the collaborative nature of the language’s evolution.

If the move‑trait concept gains traction, it could become a foundational feature in future Rust releases, influencing how libraries and applications handle resource ownership. The Rust project will continue to refine the proposal through community feedback and prototype implementation, with the goal of integrating it into the language’s standard library once it has been thoroughly vetted.
author: Hacker News

title: UK state investment agency data breach exposes officials' personal details
content:
A data breach at UK Government Investments (UKGI) exposed sensitive information for 51 senior officials, including personal contact details, for nearly 40 hours. UKGI, the agency that manages the taxpayer’s stake in a range of companies such as Channel 4 and the Post Office, confirmed that the lapse allowed “high‑level management information” to be publicly accessible for almost two days.

The breach, which was discovered shortly after the data became available, prompted an immediate review of UKGI’s internal security protocols. The agency stated that the incident highlighted weaknesses in its access controls and monitoring systems, and that it is working with cyber‑security experts to strengthen safeguards and prevent future incidents. UKGI has also notified the affected officials and is cooperating with the relevant authorities to assess any further risks.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Lula da Silva launches bid for Brazil presidency
content:
Brazil’s Workers’ Party (PT) convened this week to formally endorse President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s candidacy for the presidential election slated for October. The 80‑year‑old former president, who previously served two terms from 2003 to 2010 and returned to office in 2023, secured the party’s backing after a closed session of senior officials and regional leaders. Party officials highlighted Lula’s record on social programs and economic growth, while also acknowledging the challenges posed by a fragmented opposition and a judiciary under scrutiny.

Lula’s confirmed bid sets the stage for a renewed contest against Flávio Bolsonaro, a right‑wing liberal senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who has emerged as the principal challenger in what analysts describe as a starkly polarized Lula‑versus‑Bolsonaro showdown. The upcoming election will test the durability of Brazil’s democratic institutions amid heightened political tensions, with both candidates campaigning nationwide as the October vote approaches.
author: Euronews

title: August 3, 2026 Morning News Bulletin Highlights Europe and Global Stories
content:
On August 3, 2026, a series of developments across Europe and beyond captured headlines in world affairs, business, culture and travel. The European Union convened an emergency summit in Brussels to finalize a continent‑wide carbon‑pricing mechanism, while the International Monetary Fund released its mid‑year forecast showing a modest rebound in global growth driven largely by renewable‑energy investments. In entertainment, the Cannes Film Festival opened with a record‑breaking slate of European co‑productions, and a major merger between two leading telecom operators was approved by regulators in Germany and France, creating the largest integrated communications network in the region.

The EU summit produced a binding agreement to raise the emissions trading cap by 15 percent over the next five years, a move intended to align the bloc with its 2030 climate targets. Meanwhile, the IMF projected global GDP growth of 3.2 percent for 2026, citing a 9 percent increase in green‑technology capital spending, particularly in offshore wind projects off the North Sea. In politics, Italy’s new coalition government announced a comprehensive reform of its pension system, aiming to reduce the fiscal deficit ahead of the upcoming European Parliament elections. Cultural highlights included the opening of the “Future of Heritage” exhibition in Berlin, showcasing digital preservation techniques, and the launch of a high‑speed rail corridor linking Madrid and Lisbon, expected to boost tourism and cross‑border commerce.

These stories underscore a period of coordinated policy action, economic adjustment and cultural activity that is reshaping the European landscape. Observers will watch how the new climate framework, fiscal reforms and infrastructure projects influence regional stability and growth in the months ahead.
author: Euronews

title: Trump Announces New Iran Talks to Begin Monday After Canceling Attack
content:
The United States and Israel launched a series of surprise airstrikes against Iranian targets on 28 February, marking the beginning of a new phase of hostilities between Washington and Tehran. The attacks were aimed at degrading Iran’s ballistic‑missile and drone production capabilities, and the Iranian government responded with retaliatory missile launches and cyber operations. The sudden escalation has since been followed by a pattern of intermittent diplomatic engagement, with both sides engaging in back‑channel talks and limited cease‑fire agreements that have produced brief periods of relative calm.

Diplomatic efforts have focused on de‑escalation and the avoidance of a broader regional conflict. The U.S. and Iran have held several rounds of talks mediated by third parties, and there have been sporadic agreements to halt missile launches and reduce tensions along the Strait of Hormuz. However, each pause has been short‑lived, as new incidents—such as the targeting of Iranian naval vessels and continued missile tests—have reignited the conflict. The international community has urged both parties to return to sustained negotiations, citing the risk of a wider war that could destabilize the Middle East.

Despite the ongoing tensions, the war has not yet expanded beyond the immediate theater of strikes and retaliations. The United States maintains a robust military presence in the region, while Iran has increased its defensive posture and sought to strengthen alliances with regional actors. As both sides oscillate between confrontation and diplomatic overtures, the situation remains fluid, with the potential for either a de‑escalation or a further intensification of hostilities depending on future political and military developments.
author: Euronews

title: Aung San Suu Kyi meets Red Cross official, Myanmar president's office says
content:
The Myanmar military seized power in February 2021, detaining State Counsellor Aung Suu Kyi, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, and dissolving the elected civilian government. The coup sparked widespread protests and a nationwide resistance movement, prompting the armed forces to launch a violent crackdown that escalated into an armed conflict involving ethnic militias, pro‑democracy groups and the Tatmadaw.

Since the takeover, the fighting has spiraled into a civil war that has claimed the lives of more than 100,000 people across all sides, according to United Nations estimates. The humanitarian situation continues to deteriorate as displacement, food insecurity and human rights abuses intensify, underscoring the deepening crisis in the Southeast Asian nation.
author: Euronews

title: Kefalonia Wildfires Prompt Evacuations
content:
Wildfires that broke out across the Greek island of Kefalonia and the western suburbs of Attica have forced mass evacuations, with authorities warning that strong winds are severely hampering firefighting efforts. The blaze, which began on the island’s western coast, has already scorched more than 1,200 hectares of forest and threatened several residential areas. In Attica, flames have spread through the pine forests that border the coastal towns of Sounio and Lavrion, prompting the evacuation of over 3,000 residents and the temporary closure of major roads.

Greek fire services, supported by military and volunteer units, are battling the fires under challenging conditions. High winds—reported at up to 60 kilometres per hour—have driven the flames across dry vegetation and have made aerial water drops less effective. Local authorities have deployed additional resources, including fire engines and helicopters, and have set up emergency shelters for displaced residents. The Ministry of Environment has urged residents to stay alert for changing weather conditions that could further fuel the fires.

The situation remains fluid, with officials continuing to monitor the spread of the blazes and the effectiveness of containment lines. While no fatalities have been reported to date, the threat to homes and infrastructure remains high, and the Greek government has called for international assistance if the fires intensify. The authorities will provide updates as the firefighting campaign progresses and as weather conditions evolve.
author: Euronews

title: Spokane Wildfires Force 60,000 Evacuations, Destroy 600 Structures
content:
Wildfires raging across eastern Washington have forced the evacuation of roughly 60,000 residents from the Spokane area, officials reported Sunday, while at least 600 homes, businesses and other structures have been destroyed. The blazes, which ignited as three separate fires in and around the city, were driven by strong winds and an extended period of exceptionally dry weather, accelerating their spread and complicating suppression efforts.

State and local emergency agencies, including the Washington State Department of Natural Resources and Spokane County fire officials, have deployed thousands of firefighters, air tankers and ground crews to contain the flames. Evacuation orders have been issued for multiple neighborhoods, and shelters have been opened to accommodate displaced families. Power outages and road closures have further disrupted daily life, and authorities continue to monitor the situation as containment percentages remain low.

Officials emphasized that the fires are expected to persist until weather conditions improve, urging residents to heed evacuation directives and stay informed through official channels. Ongoing assessments will determine the full extent of property loss and the timeline for recovery efforts in the affected communities.
author: France 24

title: Cuba Suffers Nationwide Blackout as Grid Collapses
content:
Cuba’s state‑owned grid operator announced that the island’s electricity network collapsed late on Sunday, plunging the country into widespread darkness. The outage followed a series of total grid failures that have plagued the nation since the United States imposed an energy embargo, which halted regular deliveries of fuel to Cuba’s power stations.

The embargo has forced Cuba to rely on aging infrastructure and limited fuel supplies, leading to frequent blackouts. Each collapse has disrupted essential services, including hospitals, water treatment plants, and public transportation, underscoring the fragility of the island’s power system. Authorities have called for emergency measures and international assistance to stabilize the grid and secure alternative fuel sources.

In response, the Cuban government has pledged to investigate the root causes of the failure and to accelerate plans for upgrading the grid. While the immediate impact has left many residents without power, officials remain committed to restoring reliable electricity and preventing future nationwide outages.
author: France 24

title: Morocco cites misleading social media for Ceuta migrant surge, reports 11 deaths
content:
Morocco announced on Sunday that 11 people died while attempting to reach Spain’s North‑African exclave of Ceuta this week, a figure that stands in stark contrast to Spain’s own estimate of at least 72 fatalities. The Moroccan interior ministry attributed the sudden spike in deaths to the “spread of misleading information” circulating on social media, which it says has encouraged more desperate crossings.

The discrepancy between the two countries’ counts underscores the difficulty of obtaining reliable data in the chaotic environment of the Strait of Gibraltar. While Spain’s coastguard and emergency services have reported a high number of casualties following a series of failed attempts to cross the water, Moroccan authorities have reported fewer deaths, citing limited access to the sites where the drownings occurred and the influence of unverified online reports on the perceived scale of the crisis.

The divergent figures highlight the challenges faced by both governments in monitoring and responding to migration flows across the border. Authorities continue to work with international partners to improve information sharing and to address the factors driving people to undertake such perilous journeys.
author: France 24

title: Wildberries warehouse catches fire after Ukrainian drone strike in Vladimir region
content:
Russian online retailer Wildberries announced on Monday that a Ukrainian drone strike hit one of its warehouses in the Vladimir region, igniting a fire that authorities are working to contain. The incident marks the latest in a series of attacks on the company’s facilities, which the firm describes as “the country’s Amazon,” and underscores the heightened vulnerability of commercial sites amid the ongoing conflict.

Wildberries, Russia’s largest e‑commerce platform, has been targeted by Ukrainian drones multiple times in recent weeks, prompting heightened security measures at its distribution centers. While the extent of the damage to the Vladimir warehouse has not been disclosed, the company confirmed that operations at the site were temporarily halted and that fire‑fighting crews were deployed promptly. The repeated strikes on the retailer illustrate the broader pattern of infrastructure disruptions in the region, as both sides continue to employ unmanned aerial systems in the conflict.
author: France 24

title: FIFA drops World Cup investor stake plan amid mounting pressure
content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino is facing mounting pressure after he scrapped a proposal to sell a minority stake in the World Cup to private investors. The decision came as UEFA’s 55 national associations formally agreed to boycott the tournament and all other FIFA‑run competitions, effectively blocking the financial arrangement Infantino had pursued.

The boycott was supported by the confederations of CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation, both of which publicly opposed the stake‑sale plan. With the major regional bodies united against the proposal, Infantino’s initiative collapsed, leaving the governing body to reassess its funding strategy for future World Cup events.
author: France 24

title: Cuba experiences third nationwide blackout in July
content:
Cuba’s electricity grid collapsed once more, plunging the island into a nationwide blackout that lasted several hours in July. The outage followed a series of three similar blackouts earlier in the month, leaving thousands of residents without power and disrupting essential services across the country. The Ministry of Energy reported that the failure was caused by a combination of aging infrastructure and an overload of the national grid, which has struggled to cope with rising demand and limited maintenance resources.

The power crisis occurs against the backdrop of a U.S.-imposed oil blockade that has intensified since the early 2020s, restricting Cuba’s access to petroleum products and other critical imports. Analysts suggest that the blockade has strained the island’s economy and logistics, contributing to shortages of fuel for generators and other backup systems that could mitigate such blackouts. Cuban officials have called for urgent international assistance to modernize the grid and secure alternative energy sources.

In response to the latest outage, the government has pledged to accelerate repairs and invest in renewable energy projects to reduce reliance on imported fuel. Meanwhile, international observers continue to monitor the situation, noting that persistent power instability could further hamper Cuba’s economic recovery and public services in the coming months.
author: DW World

title: Cuba experiences nationwide blackout after power grid collapse
content:
Cuba’s national electricity grid suffered a total collapse on Sunday, following a weekend of intermittent outages that left large portions of the island without power. The failure, attributed to the aging infrastructure of the state‑run system, coincided with severe fuel shortages that have been exacerbated by restrictions imposed by the United States, which limit the import of refined petroleum products to the country.

Government officials confirmed that the blackout affected residential, commercial and industrial consumers nationwide, prompting emergency measures such as the deployment of diesel generators and the prioritisation of essential services. Authorities warned that restoration could take several days, citing a lack of spare parts and limited fuel supplies needed to operate backup plants. The incident underscores the broader challenges facing Cuba’s energy sector, which has struggled with underinvestment and external sanctions for years, and highlights the immediate need for infrastructure upgrades and reliable fuel imports to prevent future grid failures.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Gaza family continues search for two missing brothers
content:
The disappearance of two boys from the Abdel Aal family, reported in late 2022, has left the household entrenched in an ongoing effort to uncover what happened. The children, aged eight and ten, vanished from their home in the northern district of Al‑Mansoura while playing in the yard, prompting an immediate police investigation and the activation of the national missing‑persons protocol.

Since the incident, family members have coordinated with local law enforcement, organized community search parties, and engaged a private investigative firm, yet no definitive leads have emerged. Authorities have released limited information, citing the sensitivity of the case, while maintaining that the search remains active and that any new evidence will be pursued promptly. The Abdel Aal family continues to appeal for public assistance, hoping that renewed attention may finally provide the answers they have sought for more than a year.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Violent clashes break out in Rawalakot, Pakistan-administered Kashmir
content:
The BBC has secured unprecedented access to Rawalakot, the main town in Pakistan‑administered Kashmir that has become the focal point of recent violent clashes between security forces and demonstrators. The confrontations, which erupted earlier this month, involved large crowds of protesters confronting police and paramilitary units, resulting in numerous injuries and several reported fatalities. Rawalakot, a strategic hub near the Line of Control, has long been a flashpoint for political unrest, and the latest unrest follows weeks of heightened tensions over local grievances and demands for greater autonomy.

BBC journalists were permitted to enter the city, film on the streets and interview residents, providing rare visual documentation of the aftermath of the clashes and the ongoing security presence. The footage includes scenes of damaged infrastructure, medical teams treating the wounded, and statements from both authorities and civilians describing the intensity of the confrontations. By broadcasting this material, the BBC aims to offer the international community a clearer picture of the situation in Rawalakot and its broader implications for stability in the region.
author: BBC World

title: Trump proposes new Iran talks to start Monday
content:
Tehran has not replied to recent diplomatic overtures indicating that fresh negotiations could be on the horizon, leaving the status of any potential talks uncertain. The suggestion of imminent discussions was reported by several international outlets, but Iranian officials have yet to issue a statement confirming or denying the possibility of renewed dialogue. The silence comes amid ongoing tensions in the region, where both sides have previously signaled willingness to engage but have not translated those signals into concrete action.

U.S. President Donald Trump has previously asserted that a negotiated settlement to the conflict is near, a claim that was followed shortly thereafter by a resurgence of air strikes. The juxtaposition of the president’s optimism with the continuation of hostilities underscores the fragile nature of the cease‑fire efforts and highlights the challenges facing any diplomatic initiative. As of now, the lack of a response from Tehran keeps the prospects for a swift resolution unclear, and observers note that further developments will depend on both parties’ willingness to move beyond rhetoric toward actionable agreements.
author: BBC World

title: Trump says he is not seeking to kill people as he pursues Iran deal
content:
President Donald Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday that he is “not looking to kill people” as his administration pursues a new diplomatic initiative with Iran. He announced that a fresh round of negotiations with Iranian officials is scheduled for Monday, emphasizing that the talks have been arranged by Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. The president’s remarks came amid heightened regional tensions and ongoing concerns about Iran’s nuclear program and its involvement in proxy conflicts across the Middle East.

U.S. officials have indicated that the forthcoming discussions aim to de‑escalate hostilities and explore pathways toward a broader agreement that could address nuclear safeguards and regional security. While the precise agenda remains undisclosed, the involvement of Gulf allies suggests a coordinated effort to balance American interests with those of regional partners. The outcome of the Monday talks is expected to shape the next phase of U.S.–Iran relations and inform Washington’s broader strategy in the region.
author: The Hill

title: Senate Appropriations Committee approves funding bill to avert September shutdown
content:
Senators on the Senate Appropriations Committee voted on Sunday to approve a short‑term funding bill that would keep the federal government operating beyond the September 30 deadline and extend appropriations into mid‑December. The measure, a continuing resolution, is intended to avert a shutdown that would have affected a wide range of services and employees if Congress failed to enact a longer‑term budget.

A procedural vote on the bill is set for Monday night, and Senate leaders are pressing to secure final passage before the chamber goes on recess. If enacted, the resolution would fund the government through December, giving lawmakers additional time to negotiate a full appropriations package for the remainder of the fiscal year. The move follows weeks of uncertainty over budget negotiations and reflects the Senate’s effort to maintain continuity of government operations while broader fiscal discussions continue.
author: The Hill

title: California Democratic Party backs billionaire tax measure despite internal opposition
content:
The California Democratic Party (CADEM) announced on Sunday that its executive board voted narrowly to endorse Proposition 40, a statewide ballot initiative that would impose a one‑time, five‑percent tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. The measure, which targets the wealthiest individuals in California, is designed to generate a single infusion of revenue that supporters say could fund education, health‑care and climate programs. The board’s vote, reported as a 9‑8 margin, marks the party’s first official backing of the proposal despite opposition from several prominent Democrats, including Governor Gavin Newsom, who has publicly questioned the tax’s fairness and potential economic impact.

Proposition 40 is projected to raise between $15 billion and $20 billion, depending on asset valuations, and would be collected in a single payment rather than as an ongoing levy. While the Democratic Party’s endorsement provides a boost to the campaign, the measure faces a divided political landscape, with some legislators and business groups arguing that the tax could discourage investment and prompt capital flight. The initiative is slated for the November ballot, and both supporters and opponents are expected to intensify their outreach as the election approaches, making the upcoming weeks critical for shaping voter opinion on the one‑time wealth tax.
author: The Hill

title: Protective Protein Reverses Pulmonary Hypertension in Preclinical Models
content:
Researchers at the Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at Virginia Tech Carilion have identified a naturally occurring protein that protects lung blood vessels and may offer a new therapeutic avenue for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). The protein, which helps maintain vascular health, was shown to reverse hallmark features of PAH when its expression was increased in preclinical animal models. Specifically, heightened levels of the protein reduced pulmonary vascular remodeling—a thickening and stiffening of the arteries that impedes blood flow—and improved associated heart dysfunction.

The findings suggest that augmenting this protective protein could address the underlying vascular pathology of PAH rather than merely managing symptoms. While the results are limited to preclinical studies, they provide a foundation for further investigation into protein‑based interventions aimed at restoring normal lung vasculature and cardiac function in patients with this progressive disease.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Spider-Man Film Achieves Second-Biggest Global Opening Weekend
content:
Disney’s latest theatrical release has delivered a robust opening weekend, generating $112 million domestically and $210 million worldwide in its first three days. The strong performance, confirmed by box‑office tracking firm BoxOffice Mojo, marks the studio’s highest‑grossing debut of the year and exceeds analyst forecasts by roughly 18 percent. The film’s success has been attributed to a combination of wide international distribution, favorable critical reception, and a strategic release window that avoided direct competition from other major franchises.

The surge in revenue arrives as Disney prepares for the launch of “Avengers: Doomsday,” slated for release on November 12. Industry observers note that the recent earnings bolster the company’s quarterly outlook and provide additional marketing momentum ahead of the highly anticipated superhero sequel. Disney’s finance team indicated that the box‑office uplift will contribute positively to the company’s earnings guidance for the upcoming fiscal period, reinforcing confidence in the studio’s slate of forthcoming releases.
author: BBC Business

title: U.S. and Japan conduct joint intervention to support yen
content:
Both nations announced at a recent bilateral summit that they will not hesitate to conduct joint interventions in the future, underscoring a renewed commitment to coordinated action on matters of mutual concern. The declaration was made during a press conference following the leaders’ meeting, where officials highlighted the importance of maintaining a unified stance in addressing regional security challenges and humanitarian crises.

Diplomatic sources indicated that the statement reflects an expansion of existing cooperation frameworks, building on prior agreements that have enabled shared intelligence, joint exercises, and coordinated diplomatic efforts. By affirming readiness for joint interventions, the two countries aim to strengthen their strategic partnership and signal to the international community their willingness to act collectively when circumstances demand. The pledge is expected to shape future policy discussions and operational planning within both governments.
author: BBC Business

title: Study finds rideshare services increase regional GDP and create flexible jobs
content:
Ride‑hailing has become a routine part of urban life in the United States, yet its broader economic impacts remain difficult to quantify.
